clinical_knowledge.topic: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's disease vs Ulcerative Colitis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's disease vs Ulcerative Colitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Urgent outpatient or inpatient workup: bloods, stool studies, colonoscopy referral, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhoea for 8 months

Key HPI features: crampy lower abdominal pain, worse before bowel movements, relieved slightly after, 4-6 loose stools per day, occasional blood and mucus, 6kg unintentional weight loss, fatigue, no fever currently
Objective/Exam findings: Needs FBC (anaemia?), CRP/ESR, calprotectin, stool culture/MC&S, colonoscopy with biopsy.
Relevant background/PMH: appendicectomy at 19, no other medical history
Current medications: none regular, occasional ibuprofen for period pain
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's disease vs Ulcerative Colitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Infective colitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Blood and mucus in the stool with unintentional weight loss.
management_principles: Urgent outpatient or inpatient workup: bloods, stool studies, colonoscopy referral
Address cancer anxiety with reassurance and plan
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 34F with 8-month history of crampy lower abdominal pain, 4-6 loose stools/day with blood and mucus, 6kg weight loss, fatigue. Stress attributed by patient. No travel hx. Takes ibuprofen occasionally.
reference_soap.objective: Needs FBC (anaemia?), CRP/ESR, calprotectin, stool culture/MC&S, colonoscopy with biopsy.
reference_soap.assessment: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's vs UC) most likely. DDx: infective colitis, IBS (diagnosis of exclusion), colorectal malignancy (less likely at 34 but must exclude), coeliac disease.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent outpatient or inpatient workup: bloods, stool studies, colonoscopy referral. Advise stopping NSAIDs. Address cancer anxiety with reassurance and plan. GI referral.

learning_objectives: Characterise lower GI symptoms systematically (SOCRATES for pain, stool chart features)
Identify red flag symptoms: PR blood, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms
Provide structured cancer reassurance while arranging appropriate investigation

teaching.diagnosis: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's disease vs Ulcerative Colitis)
teaching.one_liner: Chronic autoimmune inflammation of the bowel wall causes cramping, bloody diarrhoea, and weight loss; Crohn's and ulcerative colitis are the two main types.
red_flags: Blood and mucus in the stool with unintentional weight loss

must_ask.say: Have you noticed any blood or mucus mixed in with your stool?
Does the cramping ease off once you've had a bowel movement?
How many times a day do you go, and is it loose or watery?
Have you lost weight without trying to?
Do the bowel movements ever wake you up at night, and have you been more tired than usual?
Have you had any fevers along with this?
Have you traveled anywhere recently, or eaten something that might have been contaminated?

history.answer: I've been suffering from terrible stomach cramps and loose, watery stools on and off for about eight months now.
It started gradually about eight months ago, and instead of clearing up, it has been persistent and getting slightly worse.
I pass loose, watery stools about four to six times every day.
Yes, I've noticed streaks of bright red blood and slimy mucus mixed in my stool a couple of times a week.
Yes, I often wake up once or twice during the night feeling an urgent need to run to the toilet.
The pain is a crampy feeling across my lower belly that builds up before I have to go, and it eases a bit right after bowel movements.
Yes, I constantly feel this sudden, urgent pressure to rush to the bathroom even when there isn't much to pass.
No, I haven't had any fever or shivering, just feeling exhausted.
No nausea or vomiting, my stomach holds food down without any trouble.
I haven't felt faint or dizzy, and my mouth isn't dry because I make sure to drink water throughout the day.
No, I haven't eaten any suspicious raw foods or seafood, and nobody around me has been sick.
No, I haven't travelled overseas or gone camping anywhere recently.
No, I haven't taken any antibiotics or been admitted to a hospital in years.
Yes, I have unintentionally lost about 6 kilograms over the past eight months without dieting.
No specific food seems to cause it, whether I avoid dairy or wheat, the diarrhea stays the same.
My job in finance is very high-stress, but the diarrhea happens constantly regardless of how busy my week is, and I never get constipated.
No joint aches, skin rashes, mouth ulcers, or red painful eyes at all.
No heart palpitations, heat intolerance, or sudden facial flushing.
I've been feeling completely worn out and drained of energy for the last few months.
Because work has been so stressful, I kept telling myself it might just be irritable bowel syndrome.
I saw the blood in the toilet bowl and looked it up online, so I'm terrified that it could be bowel cancer.
I really hope to find out what's causing this and get medication to stop the diarrhea so I can get through my workday.
I have no long-term medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or asthma.
I had my appendix removed when I was nineteen, but no other operations or hospitalizations since.
I don't take any regular prescribed medicines, just occasional ibuprofen tablets when I get bad period cramps.
No, I do not have any known allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two glasses of wine on the weekend.
I work as a financial analyst in an office, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
No one in my family has had bowel cancer, Crohn's disease, or ulcerative colitis as far as I know.
My last period was two weeks ago, my monthly cycle is regular, and I just get mild cramps on the first day.
We use condoms consistently for birth control, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, pulse 78 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert young woman appearing somewhat fatigued, sitting comfortably with no acute distress.
Mild conjunctival pallor present; sclerae are anicteric.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink with no aphthous ulcers or mucosal lesions.
Normal skin turgor with no rashes, erythema nodosum, or pyoderma gangrenosum lesions.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended with a well-healed right lower quadrant scar from previous appendicectomy.
Hyperactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on palpation across the lower quadrants, most noticeable in the left lower quadrant; no palpable masses.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary guarding in any abdominal quadrant.
No perianal skin tags, fistulae, or fissures; mild rectal wall tenderness, no masses, and traces of mucus with streaks of red blood visible on the examining glove.
No peripheral joint swelling, warmth, or tenderness, with full range of motion preserved.
